registers.role: controls: income, permanent income, liquid assets, debt service, disposable income

variables_mentioned: spending share of the SP payout
expected effect of the 2010 tax reform

registers.role: descriptive evidence that the policy was unanticipated (Figure 1)
variables_mentioned: number of articles about the SP savings scheme in national newspapers

linkages: Survey respondents are joined at the individual level to third-party reported administrative register data from the Danish Tax Agency (SKAT) and to other administrative registers.
Interview persons are linked to spouses or partners so that account-specific interest rates can be aggregated to a household marginal interest rate.
The survey sample was drawn at random from the ATP register of all SP account holders.
The 2012 follow-up survey re-contacted 3,116 persons from the original survey and added randomly selected new respondents; the responses were matched to the 2008 marginal interest rates.

sample.universe: All individuals with a Special Pension (SP) account in Denmark: 2,603,565 individuals, corresponding to 70 percent of the adult population (25 years and older); 94 percent chose to have their funds paid out.
sample.unit_of_observation: Individual survey respondent, with liquidity variables computed at the household level (respondent plus spouse/partner).
selection_rules: Respondents sampled at random from the entire set of SP account holders.
Telephone interviews conducted in weeks 4-7 of January 2010; response rate 50 percent including item nonresponse.

5,037 completed interviews in which the respondent stated that the SP balance had been taken out; 215 respondents who did not take out the funds are excluded from the main analysis (they are included as nonspenders in a robustness check, Online Appendix Table EA.7).
Figure 7 additionally omits self-employed persons, persons with an SP payment smaller than 1,000 DKK and persons under 25 years of age (4,388 observations).
Figure 5 uses the subsample of 1,425-1,426 observations for which financial institutions report an actual loan interest rate.
Figure 6, panel B uses 4,898 observations; Figure 9 uses the January 2012 follow-up survey (5,866 respondents in the text, 5,868 observations in the figure note).
sample.period: Register variables for 2008 (income history 1998-2008; accounts 2007-2009); SP payout 1 June - 31 December 2009; survey January 2010; follow-up survey January 2012.
sample.n_observations: 5,037 completed interviews (4,388 in Figure 7; 4,898 in Figure 6 panel B; 1,426 in Figure 5; 5,868 in Figure 9)

construction_notes: Account-specific interest rate: r_h,l = R^08_h,l / (0.5 * [D^07_h,l + D^08_h,l]), where R^08 is interest payments on account l during 2008 and D^07, D^08 are the end-2007 and end-2008 balances.
Only loans with a balance of at least 1,000 DKK are included.
Household marginal interest rate: the highest account-specific loan rate if the household has at least one loan account; otherwise the smallest account-specific deposit rate.
Mortgage loans are excluded from the reported marginal interest rate; including them leaves the results practically identical.
Interest rates are computed at the household level (the respondent linked to spouse/partner); individual-level calculations did not affect the results.
Propensity to spend: the amount the respondent says was spent out of the SP payout, divided by the total payout, in percent.
The mean net-of-tax payout in the sample is 11.200 DKK; the average gross payout in the population was 15,447 DKK and the average net payout 9,536 DKK.
Permanent income is the average of incomes over the period 1998-2008.
Liquid assets include deposits, shares and bonds; debt service denotes total interest payments on loans.
Register spending is imputed as c_it = y_it - delta W_it - p_it (disposable income minus the change in net bank assets minus pension contributions), following Browning and Leth-Petersen (2003).
In equation (7) the register and survey measures are normalized on the level of the SP payout and the dependent variable is transformed into the dummy 1[z^R_it > m(z^R_it)].

Threshold dummies: liquid assets worth less than one month's disposable income; debt service of 15 percent or more of disposable income. Thresholds were chosen by experimenting and picking the most predictive values.

claims.statement: Households with a higher pre-policy (2008) marginal interest rate report spending a larger share of the 2009 SP stimulus payout (bivariate regression).

register_source.value: Danish Tax Agency (SKAT) raw account-level files on every individual deposit and loan account, 2007-2009 (no DST register code given in the paper)

definition.value: The interest rate at which the household can access additional liquidity, computed for 2008 from third-party-reported account-level data: an account-specific rate is 2008 interest payments on loan l divided by the average of the end-2007 and end-2008 balance; for households with loan accounts (balance at least 1,000 DKK) the marginal rate is the highest such loan rate, for deposit-only households the smallest deposit rate. Computed at the household level, mortgage loans excluded.

timing.value: Measured in 2008, the year before the policy was announced (1 March 2009) and paid out.

outcome.label: Spending share in percent of SP payout (propensity to spend)

register_source.value: Survey only (Epinion A/S telephone survey, January 2010); spending is not recorded in the administrative registers

definition.value: Self-reported marginal propensity to spend: the part of the 2009 SP (Special Pension) payout that the respondent states was allocated to increased spending, put in proportion to the total payout and expressed in percent of the payout. The survey asked respondents to allocate the increase in the sum of money at their disposal in 2009 between increased spending, increased free savings, debt reduction and increased pension savings.

timing.value: Spending during calendar year 2009 attributed by the respondent to the SP payout (payouts ran 1 June-31 December 2009); elicited in the telephone survey in weeks 4-7 of January 2010.

units.value: percentage points of the spending share (percent of the SP payout) per 1 percentage point of the 2008 marginal interest rate

magnitude.interpretation: a 1 percentage point increase in the marginal interest rate is associated with an increase in the propensity to spend of 0.5 percentage points

estimand.target_population: Danish SP account holders who took out their SP balance in 2009, as represented by the survey sample; the paper frames the estimate as a predictive association, not as the causal effect of changing a household's marginal interest rate.
estimand.time_horizon: Spending during calendar year 2009 attributed to the SP payout, reported in January 2010.

population.description: Danish individuals with a Special Pension (SP) account who were drawn at random from the full set of SP account holders, completed the January 2010 telephone survey and stated that they had taken out their SP balance (5,037 respondents), linked at the individual/household level to administrative registers.
population.period: SP payout 1 June-31 December 2009; survey January 2010; register variables for 2008 (income history 1998-2008)
population.selection: Random sample of SP account holders; 50 percent response rate including item nonresponse; restricted to respondents who took out the SP balance (215 respondents who did not take out the funds are excluded from the main sample). Nonrespondents are slightly younger, more often single, more often renters, with lower income and smaller SP accounts; these differences are statistically significant but quantitatively small.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across households in pre-policy (2008) register-measured characteristics, combined with the unanticipated Danish SP payout announced 1 March 2009, which let SP account holders convert illiquid pension wealth into liquid wealth between 1 June and 31 December 2009. The regressor is not randomised; the paper reports predictive associations.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents understand the counterfactual nature of the survey question, so that the reported allocation of the SP payout to spending reflects the causal effect of the payout on spending rather than the respondent's usual level of spending.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of the survey answers with register measures of net saving, pension saving and imputed spending for 2005-2011 (equation (7), Figure 7): the slope on the survey measure is markedly larger in 2009 than in the other years.

key_assumptions.assumption: The stimulus policy was unanticipated, so that the marginal interest rate measured in 2008 is not influenced by the change in liquidity brought about by the 2009 payout.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1: media coverage of the SP scheme shows no mention of the scheme between early February 2009 and the announcement on 1 March 2009.

key_assumptions.assumption: Survey participation is ignorable for the estimates: respondents and nonrespondents differ only slightly on register characteristics, and inverse-propensity reweighting on 2008 register characteristics does not change the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix Tables EA.1 and EA.2: characterisation of respondents versus nonrespondents from population-wide registers and inverse-probability-weighted re-estimation.

key_assumptions.assumption: The computed marginal interest rate measures the household's true cost of marginal liquidity; measurement error from imputing account-specific rates is limited.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 5: the calculated marginal interest rate is compared with the interest rate reported by financial institutions for the subsample where that information exists, and the two match well. The authors note that discouraged borrowers may effectively face a higher rate than computed (footnote 10).

threats_discussed: Measurement error in the imputed marginal interest rate (addressed with Figure 5 and with the alternative interest-rate measures in Table 2).

Discouraged borrowers may effectively face a higher marginal interest rate than the one computed from realised interest payments (footnote 10); a survey question on rejected loan applications was insignificant and did not change the results.

The realized marginal interest rate might just be picking up variation in income across the persons/households in the sample (addressed with income controls, income polynomials and income-quartile splits).
People may not order accounts by liquidity cost in the assumed way (addressed with the interest-range and average-interest-rate specifications in Table 2).
The credit card puzzle: households holding expensive debt and low-return deposits simultaneously (Table 2, columns 2 and 3).
Survey nonresponse (Online Appendix Tables EA.1-EA.2).
OLS with a dependent variable that is mostly 0 or 100 (addressed with probit and tobit in Online Appendix Table EA.4).
robustness_checks: Alternative marginal interest rate definitions: subsample with both deposits and loans, deposit rates set to zero, interest range, balance-weighted average rate (Table 2).
Conventional liquidity-constraint proxies in continuous and threshold-dummy form (Table 3).
Probit and tobit instead of OLS (Online Appendix Table EA.4).
Up to fourth-order polynomials in the size of the SP payout, in all income variables and in age (Online Appendix Table EA.5).
Separate regressions by 2008 income quartile (Online Appendix Table EA.6).
Including respondents who did not take out the SP funds as nonspenders (Online Appendix Table EA.7).
Inverse-propensity weighting for survey participation (Online Appendix Table EA.2).
Interest rates computed at the individual rather than the household level, and with mortgage loans included (text, footnote 9 and page 362).
unresolved_confounders: Discouraged borrowers: people may be discouraged from borrowing and therefore effectively face a higher interest rate than the one calculated.
Lack of precision on the expected-constraint indicators cannot be distinguished from lack of variation in those indicators (footnote 13).
Insufficient statistical power to tell whether people holding both deposit accounts and loans behave differently (Table 2, column 2).

estimation.specification: Bivariate OLS of the spending share on the 2008 marginal interest rate (Table 1, column 1).
estimation.clustering: None reported; robust standard errors are reported in parentheses.

heterogeneity.finding: Separate regressions by income quartile (Online Appendix Table EA.6): the estimated effect of the interest gradient is almost identical across the four subsamples.

heterogeneity.dimension: Households holding both deposit accounts and loans
heterogeneity.finding: Table 2, column 2: the coefficient on the marginal interest rate is 0.204 with a standard error of 0.178 in this subsample; the confidence interval spans zero but also spans the full-sample estimate.

claims.statement: On average households report spending 65 percent of the SP stimulus payout.

treatment.label: SP payout received in 2009 (the stimulus payment)

register_source.value: ATP register of SP accounts; payout administered by the public pension fund ATP

definition.value: The 2009 Special Pension payout: the balance of the individual's compulsory SP pension account, paid out net of a 35-50 percent tax between 1 June and 31 December 2009 after the unanticipated announcement on 1 March 2009; the policy converted illiquid pension wealth into liquid wealth without changing lifetime resources.

timing.value: Announced 1 March 2009, paid out 1 June - 31 December 2009; 94 percent of account holders took the money out.

outcome.label: Spending share in percent of SP payout (propensity to spend)

register_source.value: Survey only (Epinion A/S telephone survey, January 2010); spending is not recorded in the administrative registers

definition.value: Self-reported marginal propensity to spend: the part of the 2009 SP (Special Pension) payout that the respondent states was allocated to increased spending, put in proportion to the total payout and expressed in percent of the payout. The survey asked respondents to allocate the increase in the sum of money at their disposal in 2009 between increased spending, increased free savings, debt reduction and increased pension savings.

timing.value: Spending during calendar year 2009 attributed by the respondent to the SP payout (payouts ran 1 June-31 December 2009); elicited in the telephone survey in weeks 4-7 of January 2010.

units.value: percent of the net-of-tax SP payout allocated to increased spending

magnitude.interpretation: the average propensity to spend out of the SP payout is 65 percent; 63 percent indicate that they spent everything and 33 percent that they spent nothing

estimand.target_population: Danish SP account holders who took out their SP balance in 2009 (94 percent of the 2,603,565 account holders chose to have the funds paid out).
estimand.time_horizon: Spending during calendar year 2009 attributed to the SP payout, reported in January 2010.

population.description: Danish individuals with a Special Pension (SP) account who were drawn at random from the full set of SP account holders, completed the January 2010 telephone survey and stated that they had taken out their SP balance (5,037 respondents), linked at the individual/household level to administrative registers.
population.period: SP payout 1 June-31 December 2009; survey January 2010; register variables for 2008 (income history 1998-2008)
population.selection: Random sample of SP account holders; 50 percent response rate including item nonresponse; restricted to respondents who took out the SP balance (215 respondents who did not take out the funds are excluded from the main sample). Nonrespondents are slightly younger, more often single, more often renters, with lower income and smaller SP accounts; these differences are statistically significant but quantitatively small.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across households in pre-policy (2008) register-measured characteristics, combined with the unanticipated Danish SP payout announced 1 March 2009. The regressor is not randomised; the paper reports predictive associations.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents understand the counterfactual nature of the survey question, so that the reported allocation of the SP payout to spending reflects the causal effect of the payout on spending rather than the respondent's usual level of spending.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of the survey answers with register measures of net saving, pension saving and imputed spending for 2005-2011 (equation (7), Figure 7): the slope on the survey measure is markedly larger in 2009 than in the other years.

key_assumptions.assumption: The stimulus policy was unanticipated, so that the marginal interest rate measured in 2008 is not influenced by the change in liquidity brought about by the 2009 payout.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1: media coverage of the SP scheme shows no mention of the scheme between early February 2009 and the announcement on 1 March 2009.

key_assumptions.assumption: Survey participation is ignorable for the estimates: respondents and nonrespondents differ only slightly on register characteristics, and inverse-propensity reweighting on 2008 register characteristics does not change the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix Tables EA.1 and EA.2: characterisation of respondents versus nonrespondents from population-wide registers and inverse-probability-weighted re-estimation.

key_assumptions.assumption: The computed marginal interest rate measures the household's true cost of marginal liquidity; measurement error from imputing account-specific rates is limited.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 5: the calculated marginal interest rate is compared with the interest rate reported by financial institutions for the subsample where that information exists, and the two match well. The authors note that discouraged borrowers may effectively face a higher rate than computed (footnote 10).

threats_discussed: Measurement error in the imputed marginal interest rate (addressed with Figure 5 and with the alternative interest-rate measures in Table 2).

Discouraged borrowers may effectively face a higher marginal interest rate than the one computed from realised interest payments (footnote 10); a survey question on rejected loan applications was insignificant and did not change the results.

The realized marginal interest rate might just be picking up variation in income across the persons/households in the sample (addressed with income controls, income polynomials and income-quartile splits).
People may not order accounts by liquidity cost in the assumed way (addressed with the interest-range and average-interest-rate specifications in Table 2).
The credit card puzzle: households holding expensive debt and low-return deposits simultaneously (Table 2, columns 2 and 3).
Survey nonresponse (Online Appendix Tables EA.1-EA.2).
OLS with a dependent variable that is mostly 0 or 100 (addressed with probit and tobit in Online Appendix Table EA.4).
robustness_checks: Alternative marginal interest rate definitions: subsample with both deposits and loans, deposit rates set to zero, interest range, balance-weighted average rate (Table 2).
Conventional liquidity-constraint proxies in continuous and threshold-dummy form (Table 3).
Probit and tobit instead of OLS (Online Appendix Table EA.4).
Up to fourth-order polynomials in the size of the SP payout, in all income variables and in age (Online Appendix Table EA.5).
Separate regressions by 2008 income quartile (Online Appendix Table EA.6).
Including respondents who did not take out the SP funds as nonspenders (Online Appendix Table EA.7).
Inverse-propensity weighting for survey participation (Online Appendix Table EA.2).
Interest rates computed at the individual rather than the household level, and with mortgage loans included (text, footnote 9 and page 362).
unresolved_confounders: Discouraged borrowers: people may be discouraged from borrowing and therefore effectively face a higher interest rate than the one calculated.
Lack of precision on the expected-constraint indicators cannot be distinguished from lack of variation in those indicators (footnote 13).
Insufficient statistical power to tell whether people holding both deposit accounts and loans behave differently (Table 2, column 2).

population.description: Respondents to the January 2012 follow-up survey: 3,116 persons from the original survey supplemented with randomly selected new respondents, 5,866 respondents in total, matched to the 2008 marginal interest rates.
population.period: SP payout 1 June-31 December 2009; survey January 2010; register variables for 2008 (income history 1998-2008)
population.selection: Random sample of SP account holders; 50 percent response rate including item nonresponse; restricted to respondents who took out the SP balance (215 respondents who did not take out the funds are excluded from the main sample). Nonrespondents are slightly younger, more often single, more often renters, with lower income and smaller SP accounts; these differences are statistically significant but quantitatively small.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across households in pre-policy (2008) register-measured characteristics, combined with the unanticipated Danish SP payout announced 1 March 2009. The regressor is not randomised; the paper reports predictive associations.

key_assumptions.assumption: Respondents understand the counterfactual nature of the survey question, so that the reported allocation of the SP payout to spending reflects the causal effect of the payout on spending rather than the respondent's usual level of spending.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Comparison of the survey answers with register measures of net saving, pension saving and imputed spending for 2005-2011 (equation (7), Figure 7): the slope on the survey measure is markedly larger in 2009 than in the other years.

key_assumptions.assumption: The stimulus policy was unanticipated, so that the marginal interest rate measured in 2008 is not influenced by the change in liquidity brought about by the 2009 payout.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1: media coverage of the SP scheme shows no mention of the scheme between early February 2009 and the announcement on 1 March 2009.

key_assumptions.assumption: Survey participation is ignorable for the estimates: respondents and nonrespondents differ only slightly on register characteristics, and inverse-propensity reweighting on 2008 register characteristics does not change the results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix Tables EA.1 and EA.2: characterisation of respondents versus nonrespondents from population-wide registers and inverse-probability-weighted re-estimation.

key_assumptions.assumption: The computed marginal interest rate measures the household's true cost of marginal liquidity; measurement error from imputing account-specific rates is limited.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 5: the calculated marginal interest rate is compared with the interest rate reported by financial institutions for the subsample where that information exists, and the two match well. The authors note that discouraged borrowers may effectively face a higher rate than computed (footnote 10).

threats_discussed: Measurement error in the imputed marginal interest rate (addressed with Figure 5 and with the alternative interest-rate measures in Table 2).

Discouraged borrowers may effectively face a higher marginal interest rate than the one computed from realised interest payments (footnote 10); a survey question on rejected loan applications was insignificant and did not change the results.

The realized marginal interest rate might just be picking up variation in income across the persons/households in the sample (addressed with income controls, income polynomials and income-quartile splits).
People may not order accounts by liquidity cost in the assumed way (addressed with the interest-range and average-interest-rate specifications in Table 2).
The credit card puzzle: households holding expensive debt and low-return deposits simultaneously (Table 2, columns 2 and 3).
Survey nonresponse (Online Appendix Tables EA.1-EA.2).
OLS with a dependent variable that is mostly 0 or 100 (addressed with probit and tobit in Online Appendix Table EA.4).
robustness_checks: Alternative marginal interest rate definitions: subsample with both deposits and loans, deposit rates set to zero, interest range, balance-weighted average rate (Table 2).
Conventional liquidity-constraint proxies in continuous and threshold-dummy form (Table 3).
Probit and tobit instead of OLS (Online Appendix Table EA.4).
Up to fourth-order polynomials in the size of the SP payout, in all income variables and in age (Online Appendix Table EA.5).
Separate regressions by 2008 income quartile (Online Appendix Table EA.6).
Including respondents who did not take out the SP funds as nonspenders (Online Appendix Table EA.7).
Inverse-propensity weighting for survey participation (Online Appendix Table EA.2).
Interest rates computed at the individual rather than the household level, and with mortgage loans included (text, footnote 9 and page 362).
unresolved_confounders: Discouraged borrowers: people may be discouraged from borrowing and therefore effectively face a higher interest rate than the one calculated.
Lack of precision on the expected-constraint indicators cannot be distinguished from lack of variation in those indicators (footnote 13).
Insufficient statistical power to tell whether people holding both deposit accounts and loans behave differently (Table 2, column 2).
